01 · The core idea

Human-led, agent-operated

People set intent, own outcomes and decide where not to automate. Agents operate inside limits people set.

Neither half works alone. Agents without human intent automate the wrong work. Intent without agents leaves the value on the table. The book makes the idea testable: every agent has a named owner, every step has a level on one scale, and the controls that enforce both belong to the enterprise.

The book’s thesis sits underneath every chapter: autonomy is earned when value compounds faster than risk. Some work adds risk faster than any agent adds value, so it stays with people.

The ten-line charter

  1. People set intent and own outcomes; agents operate inside limits people set.
  2. Every agent has a named human owner with the authority to stop it. Accountability sits with executives, never with a model or a vendor.
  3. Autonomy is set per step, earned on evidence and taken back by rule.
  4. What an agent can do never decides what it may do. Irreversible and outward-facing actions stay behind human gates.
  5. Use the simplest engine that works: rules before models, workflows before agents.
  6. Every action leaves a trace: who acted, for whom, under which policy, with what evidence.
  7. Every human override is a labeled error the program learns from.
  8. People decide where not to automate, and that list is reviewed like any other control.
  9. The enterprise owns its controls, context, definitions, skills and traces; models are replaceable parts.
  10. Autonomy is earned when value compounds faster than risk, read each period on one page.

How this changes roles, teams and decision rights: Organization: humans and agents.

02 · One shared language

The autonomy scale, L0 to L5

Autonomy is set per step, not per agent or per process. One numbered scale gives the business, auditors and the program one language for targets, controls and evidence.

LevelWho decidesWho executesHuman role
L0 ManualHumanHumanDoes the work. Right for rare, high-judgment events.
L1 AssistHumanHumanUses the agent’s suggestions. Risk: over-trust.
L2 ApproveAgent proposesAgent, after approvalApproves every action with evidence in view. Risk: rubber-stamping.
L3 Act within limitsAgentAgentHandles exceptions above limits; samples in-limit actions.
L4 Run and reportAgentAgentAudits outcomes, tunes limits and policies.
L5 FullAgentAgentSets goals only. A boundary marker, not a target, for financial postings.

Try it · The autonomy slider

L3 is the main target for high-volume transactional work, and most measurable value in the first years comes from moving work from L2 to L3. At L3 the limits on amount, risk score, counterparty class and confidence sit outside the model, never in the prompt, and the agent cannot change them.

One counter-intuitive finding: human hours can rise slightly from L2 to L3, because the items that escalate are the hardest ones. The value at L3 comes from speed and from freeing people for hard cases, not only from hours saved.

Set levels per step in the workflow designer

03 · Where each step should sit

Materiality and reversibility set the default ceiling

Two properties decide how far a step can safely go: how much damage one wrong action can do, and how easily it can be caught and undone.

Materiality per actionEasily reversibleHard to reverseIrreversible
Low (under $5,000)Up to L4Up to L3Up to L2
Medium ($5,000 to $250,000)Up to L3Up to L2L1 to L2
High (over $250,000) or regulatoryUp to L2L1 to L2L0 to L1

Try it · Find a step’s ceiling

Then five modifiers lower it

  1. Data quality. If the input data fails its quality gate, cap the step at L2.
  2. Regulation. A high-risk use under law, or a key financial control, stays at L2 until legal and audit approve more.
  3. Evidence. No step rises until it meets the exit criteria of its current level.
  4. External counterparty. If the action commits the company to a third party, lower the ceiling one level for the first 90 days.
  5. Weakest link. A step that depends on a handoff between platforms cannot run above that handoff.

Thresholds are illustrative. The book asks each company to set its own with internal audit.

Compute ceilings for your own workflow in the designer

04 · Promotion and demotion

Earned on evidence, taken back by rule

Every promotion needs evidence and a human gate. Demotion triggers move a step down automatically. Promotion is never automatic.

MoveMinimum evidence (illustrative)
L0 to L1Data access approved; suggestions logged; users trained; four weeks of shadow running with error at or below the human baseline.
L1 to L2Suggestions accepted at least 80% of the time over four weeks; agent identity and permissions in place.
L2 to L3At least 95% approved without edits over 1,000+ actions and three months including a quarter-end; limits enforced outside the model; kill switch tested; reversals below 0.5%; audit sign-off.
L3 to L4A strong control score; two quarter-ends at L3 with in-limit error below the human baseline; escalations within service level; drift monitoring live.
L4 to L5Board-level risk acceptance. Normally not pursued for postings.

Try it · The promotion gate

Automatic demotion triggers: an error above threshold, a failed data-quality gate, a change in the process or the model, or an audit finding. The book also separates duties: the person who approves an agent’s actions may not change the agent’s limits, instructions or tools.

Who decides each move, and the demotion rules in production: decision rights and reliability.

05 · The first rule

The harness, not the model, sets the ceiling

The model reasons; the harness governs. A modest model inside a strong harness can run a narrow step at L3 safely. A far better model next quarter would not raise the ceiling until the harness did.

That sets the order of design effort. Model choice is the easiest part to change later. Identity design, data contracts, interface boundaries and evidence stores are the hardest. Spend design effort in reverse order of changeability.

The ten-part harness

PartWhat it enforcesHow it fails safe
1 Identity and delegationOne identity per agent, acting on behalf of an accountable personNo token, no call
2 Registry and lifecycleOnly registered, active agent versions runUnregistered agent is blocked
3 Policy and limitsThresholds, segregation of duties, blackout windows, outside the modelMissing rule means escalate
4 Tool gatewayScopes, rate limits, read/write separationUnknown tool is rejected
5 Model gatewayRouting, fallback, masking, quotasFallback model or drop to L1
6 Context and memory controlsWhat may enter context; memory write rulesUntrusted content treated as data
7 Verification and approval gatesSchema checks, a checker, approval cardsFailed check goes to a person
8 Operating envelope and costDeadlines, call budgets, retries, loop guardsStop and escalate with trace
9 Decision traceWhat was seen, decided and doneIf the trace fails, the action fails
10 Evaluation, release and kill switchTest sets before release; stop an agent, a scope or the fleetKill switch tested quarterly

06 · The second rule

Agents decide; deterministic rules post

At L3 a step runs in four moves: propose, validate, route, commit.

  1. Propose. The agent proposes an action. It never writes to the books itself.
  2. Validate. Deterministic checks test the proposal: schema, data freshness, business rules.
  3. Route. A policy table, not the agent, decides whether the action is inside limits.
  4. Commit. Inside limits, a released interface commits it. Outside, a person approves with an evidence pack. Every path ends in a decision trace.

When to act alone: the decision threshold

The book gives one definition for when an agent may act without a person: act only when the expected gain beats the expected loss. If G is the gain when the action is right and L the loss when it is wrong, act when the agent’s confidence is at least L ÷ (G + L). Bigger stakes raise the bar automatically, so the same agent posts a small credit and routes a large one to a person.

07 · Autonomy across many systems

A chain runs only as high as its weakest link

Real work crosses ERPs, SaaS platforms, a mainframe and hundreds of interfaces. If any link needs a person to read, re-key or approve, the whole chain runs at that link’s level.

chain level = minimum (level of each step, ceiling of each handoff)

Handoff typeCeilingWhy
Manual or emailL1A person must read and act
Scheduled fileL2Hours of latency; no confirmation per record
Synchronous APIL3Real-time, authenticated, auditable per call
EventL3Real-time; needs replay and ordering controls
Governed agent toolL3Typed, authorized, traced per call
Cross-agent contractL3 to L4Defines who decides, what evidence returns and what happens on failure

Try it · Build the chain

Four decision rules follow. Fund the weakest link first. Never promise a chain level above its weakest handoff in a business case. Measure links, not only agents. Re-rate a chain whenever a link changes. The rule moves investment from agents to handoffs, which is why the book says many interfaces should be retired, not rebuilt.

08 · The economics

Compare in cost per completed outcome

Platforms now charge for agent work. A cheap action that leaves a person to finish the job is not cheap.

cost per completed outcome = platform meter charges + model and runtime charges + review minutes × loaded rate + fallback share × fallback minutes × loaded rate

Comparing on this one basis puts agents, people and vendors side by side honestly. The book’s worked examples show that delay, not the meter price, moves value most: faster decisions, fewer penalties and released working capital often outweigh hours saved.

09 · The decision programs skip

When not to automate

Deciding where not to automate is a control, not a matter of taste. A capable agent kept at L2 beside a person is often the higher-value design, not the timid one.

Keep a person deciding when…Why
The judgment is the productThe value lies in a person deciding and being seen to decide
Nobody can explain the workflowReviewers cannot challenge what they cannot describe
The error is irreversible and unboundedNo limit outside the model caps the loss
The process is about to changeAutomation freezes the old design
The data cannot carry the decisionThe quality gate failed or there is no data owner
The law reserves it to peopleSome decisions about people must have human oversight

Try it · The do-not-automate check

Across every domain the pattern holds: agents investigate, match, draft and monitor; deterministic engines compute and post; named people sign, release money and decide about safety and about people. Autonomy grows fastest where decisions are frequent, small and reversible, and stops where an action cannot be undone or a law names the signatory.

10 · Readiness

The weakest dimension caps the company

Score six dimensions from 1 to 5: core and interfaces, data and context, agents and platform, governance and controls, people and change, and value management.

The enterprise stage is the lowest score, not the average, because the weakest control sets the ceiling. Record evidence for each score and repeat every six months. The five stages run from experiments to approved autonomy, bounded autonomy and, for selected chains, autonomous operations.

The test is evidence, not ambition: a company claiming stage four with no reuse and a growing pile of open pilots is a stage-three company with more agents.

Try it · Score your company

11 · The thesis as a scorecard

The value–risk flywheel

Value and risk both compound. Raise a step’s autonomy only when its value signal is rising faster than its risk signal.

  1. Value signal. The measure that shows the step is paying off: faster decisions, cash released, cost per completed outcome falling.
  2. Risk counterweight. The measure that would hold promotion: errors, reversals, audit findings, drift. A red counterweight holds the whole agent family.
  3. Drag to remove. Some drag is good, such as a control that slows a risky action. Some is bad, such as a manual handoff that slows a safe one. Add good drag where risk leads; remove bad drag where value is blocked.

Every chapter names its value signal, risk counterweight and drag. The book turns them into a one-page scorecard read monthly per agent family and at every program gate.

Try it · Read the flywheel

12 · Making it happen

Foundations first, then a 30-month plan with gates

“A board that funds agents first and data second pays twice.” Before a layer gets a bigger budget, show evidence that the layer beneath it is ready.

  1. Data readiness. Source authority, lineage, freshness, ownership; golden records for supplier, customer and material.
  2. Platform stress test. Interfaces, events and trace stores load-tested before agents depend on them.
  3. Govern the agentic layer. Registry, identity, gateway and kill switch live before agents scale.
PhaseMonthsPurpose
0 Mobilize1–3Charter, team, baselines, architecture decisions, first shadow agents
1 Foundation and pilots4–13Platforms, data, governance plane, first interface wave, first agents to L2
2 First go-live14–19First region live; first core agents in shadow
3 Scale20–30Remaining waves; promotion and replication; decommission
4 Run31–33Handover to the line organization

Each phase closes at a gate that passes on a scorecard reading, not only on delivery milestones, so value is booked only as fast as risk is shown to be under control. The book adds a 100-day starter plan, an agent contract template, promotion checklists and board questions in its toolkit.

Figures and thresholds on this page are illustrative frameworks from the book, built around a fictional company, Meridian Industries.
